lessons.title: Hobbies
lessons.scenario: Smarty and Mia chat in the studio about what they like doing in their free time.

items.example: I am keen on music and art.
items.note: Say 'be keen on' before a noun or an -ing verb to show you really like something.

items.example: I want to take up tennis this summer.
items.note: Use 'take up' when you start a new hobby or activity.

items.example: I spend time on reading every evening.
items.note: Say 'spend time on' to talk about how you use your hours on an activity.

items.example: In my free time I play the guitar.
items.note: Use 'in my free time' to talk about what you do when you have no work or school.

items.example: I got into swimming last summer.
items.note: Say 'get into' when you start enjoying a new interest or activity.

items.example: She plays the piano as a hobby.
items.note: Add 'as a hobby' to show you do something just for fun, not as a job.

grammar.title: Talking about hobbies
grammar.explanation: Use 'be keen on', 'get into', or 'spend time on' before a noun or a verb ending in -ing. Use 'take up' when you begin a new activity.
examples: I am keen on reading in my free time.
He took up basketball as a hobby.

lessons.title: Gerund or infinitive
lessons.scenario: Leo and Mia talk about which studio projects they enjoy and want to finish.

items.example: I enjoy doing origami in the evening.
items.note: Always use a verb ending in -ing after 'enjoy', never 'to'.

items.example: I want to do pottery this weekend.
items.note: Always use 'to' plus the base verb after 'want'.

items.example: Do not give up learning the guitar.
items.note: Say 'give up' plus a noun or -ing verb when you stop trying or quit an activity.

items.example: She managed to make a small clay bowl.
items.note: Use 'manage to' plus a base verb when you succeed in doing something difficult.

items.example: I would like to learn embroidery.
items.note: Say 'would like to' plus a base verb to politely express a wish or plan.

items.example: Keep on practising and it gets easy.
items.note: Use 'keep on' plus an -ing verb when you continue doing something without stopping.

grammar.title: Gerund (-ing) or infinitive (to + verb)
grammar.explanation: After 'enjoy', 'give up', and 'keep on', use the -ing form of the next verb. After 'want', 'manage', and 'would like', use 'to' plus the base verb.
examples: I enjoy knitting, so I keep on making scarves.
I would like to learn sewing, and I want to make a bag.

practice.prompt: Which sentence uses the right pattern after 'enjoy'?
practice.answer: I enjoy knitting in my free time.
options: I enjoy knitting in my free time.
I enjoy to knit in my free time.
I enjoy knit in my free time.
practice.explanation: Use the -ing form (knitting) after 'enjoy'.

practice.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
practice.answer: Leo would like to learn woodwork.
options: Leo would like to learn woodwork.
practice.explanation: Use 'to' plus the base verb ('to learn') after 'would like'.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.audio: Mia managed to make a small cup.
practice.answer: Mia managed to make a small cup.
options: Mia managed to make a small cup.
Mia gave up on the small cup.
Mia wants to buy a small cup.
practice.explanation: 'Managed to' means she succeeded even though it was hard.

practice.prompt: Match the first half of each sentence with the right ending.
practice.explanation: 'Enjoy' and 'give up' take -ing; 'would like' and 'manage' take 'to + verb'.

practice.prompt: Build the encouraging sentence.

practice.explanation: Use 'want to do' to ask about someone's plan or wish.

practice.answer: I enjoy doing origami and I would like to learn pottery.
practice.explanation: Notice 'enjoy doing' (-ing) and 'would like to learn' (to + verb).

lessons.title: How long have you been?
lessons.scenario: Smarty asks Ben how long he has been practising his hobbies in the studio.

items.example: I have been learning pottery since autumn.
items.note: Use 'I have been learning' for a skill you started studying in the past and still study now.

items.example: I have been playing the piano for about a year.
items.note: Say 'for about a year' when the time is close to twelve months, not an exact number.

items.example: I have been practising the guitar every day.
items.note: Use 'I have been practising' to show repeated training that is still going on.

items.example: How long have you been doing origami?
items.note: Start a question with 'How long have you been' plus an -ing verb to ask about duration.

items.example: Lately I have been spending time on woodwork.
items.note: Say 'lately I have been' to talk about a recent habit or activity over the past few days or weeks.

items.example: She has been knitting that scarf all week.
items.note: Use 'all week' to show an activity continued from the start of the week until now.

grammar.title: Present perfect continuous
grammar.explanation: Use 'have/has been + verb-ing' to talk about actions that started in the past and are still happening now. Ask with 'How long have you been + verb-ing?' and answer with 'for' or 'all week'.
examples: How long have you been learning the violin?
I have been practising for about a year.

options: How long have you been learning the guitar?

practice.prompt: Ben started pottery around twelve months ago. How does he say this?

panels.text: Look at the map! Someone drew a tower next to a river. Where does this map go?
